A peer is a term referring to a person who holds certain titles of nobility. There have been numerous changes to the British political system over the years, so the following is not going to be entirely correct as I want to make it simple without chasing down every rabbit hole.

The UK parliament has two bodies: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. You can think of them as similar to the US House of Representatives and Senate. The House of Commons is filled with people elected by the citizenry. The House of Lords is filled with people who hold titles which give them the right to be in the chamber (e.g., Duke of Flibberdigibbet or Baroness Whatshername).

There are two types of peers in the House of Lords: hereditary peers and life peers. The former are historical and the titles are passed down generationally as they have been for centuries. The latter are political appointees who are given titles which are personal to them and not passed down to heirs giving them membership in the House of Lords for life (kind of like Federal judges in the US).
